title: Box breathing
hookLine: in, hold, out, hold, four counts each, a drill used by pilots and first responders

lines: THE PARAMEDIC ON A WET ROAD.
cards: A paramedic kneeling on a wet road. A firefighter at a door with smoke under it. A pilot when a warning light comes on.
Jobs like these ask people to stay steady when everything is loud. The tool some of them are taught is so plain you could draw it on a napkin: a square, four sides, four counts each.
It's taught in some military, police and first-responder training, and it needs no cushion, no quiet room and no one's permission. Today: box breathing.

teach.b: Breathe in for four. Hold for four. Breathe out for four.
Hold for four. That's one box; then around again. Some people trace it with a finger on their knee: up one side, across the top, down, across the bottom.
Why a box, after a week of longer exhales and sighs? Two reasons.
First, the holds slow everything down. A box of fours takes sixteen seconds, just under four breaths a minute, far slower than an ordinary resting breath.

teach.h: THE COUNT GIVES THE MIND A JOB.
teach.b: Second, and maybe more important, the counting gives the mind a job. Under pressure, the mind races through what could go wrong next. Four sides and four counts leave it very little room to race.
The box is less about the air and more about the attention. It's popular partly because a former Navy SEAL officer, Mark Divine, taught it widely, and because first responders pass it to each other.
The research on box breathing itself is thinner than the stories. In the Stanford study from two days ago, box breathing was one of the groups, and it helped mood too, though less than sighing.
So it's a tool, not a miracle, and a good tool has a use.

The box is for the moment when you have to stay in the room and keep your head: before a hard call, in a waiting room, at the edge of an argument. You can do it with your eyes open and nobody will know.

how: Box breathing, four counts in, hold, out and hold, is taught in some military, police and first-responder training and in stress-management courses, often as something to do with eyes open, right before a high-pressure moment.

games.q: you're about to walk into a hard conversation and your mind is racing through what could go wrong. you have thirty seconds. what do you do?
o: rehearse your arguments one more time.
trace two boxes on your knee.
check your phone to distract yourself.
games.why: the box gives the racing mind a job and slows the breath. two boxes is about thirty seconds.

practice: Eyes open or closed, trace the square on your knee if you like: in through the nose for four, hold gently for four, out for four, hold for four, and go around four times.
If four counts is too long, use three; if the holds feel tight, make them softer. After the fourth box, let the breath go back to its own rhythm and just sit.

orig.note: Sanskrit, from yoga's breath practice: the held breath, named for a kumbha, a water pot, full and still.
